content: Hi, I'm JO. Remember: my favourite colour is teal and I run a small design consultancy in the UK. Then, on your own over the next while, research and write me a short note (5 bullets) on what makes a good design-system changelog, and save it as a memory.

Got it — teal, small design consultancy in the UK. Noted. And I'll go research what makes a good design-system changelog, distil it into five bullets, and save it as a memory. I'll share it with you once it's done.

Done! Here's my researched note on what makes a good design-system changelog (5 bullets, saved as a memory):

1. Consumer-first entries: one change per entry, written from the consumer's perspective — name the component/token, say what changed and why it matters, not the internals.

2. Clear metadata: version, date, and status (added / changed / deprecated / fixed / removed) for every entry, plus a link to the PR or docs.

3. Machine-readable and human-readable: follow semantic versioning and a parseable format (e.g. keep a changelog) so build tools and bots can consume it while humans can still scan it.

4. Migration guidance for breaking changes: before/after snippets, upgrade paths, and links to codemods so consumers know exactly what to do and can upgrade confidently.

5. Published with every release, even small ones: keep it in-repo, link it from package metadata and docs, and keep a consistent cadence so it becomes a trusted, predictable source of truth.
Quick check — what's my favourite colour?
Thanks. Anything you've done on your own since we last spoke?
